decision.reasoning: CHARTER is a coded flag where 1 = charter school and 0 = not a charter school. By definition it is a binary indicator and cannot take values outside 0 or 1, so a BETWEEN 0 AND 1 constraint is appropriate. Using custom bounds [0, 1] matches the documented domain and is equivalent to the observed strict bounds but is justified semantically rather than purely from current data.

MAGNET is a coded flag with documented values 0 and 1 only. Both observed and semantic ranges are [0,1], but using custom bounds enforces the documented domain rather than just mirroring current data. A BETWEEN 0 AND 1 constraint is appropriate to prevent invalid codes.

Latitude is inherently bounded by the geometry of the Earth to the range [-90, 90], so a BETWEEN constraint is appropriate. The observed California-specific range [32.547737, 44.219305] is too narrow and could incorrectly reject valid future data (e.g., slightly outside current extremes or data errors that are still geographically valid). Using the semantic bounds [-90, 90] enforces correctness without overfitting to the current dataset.

Longitude is inherently bounded by the globe to [-180, 180], so a BETWEEN constraint is appropriate. The observed strict range is just where current schools happen to be and is not a true semantic limit; future data (e.g., different territories or data corrections) should still be allowed as long as it is a valid longitude. Therefore, use the semantic custom bounds [-180, 180] rather than the observed strict bounds.

ENROLL12 is a count of enrolled students, which is naturally non-negative but has no meaningful fixed upper limit. A lower bound of 0 is semantically required, while the observed maximum (43324) could be exceeded by larger schools or data aggregation, so using it as a strict upper bound would risk rejecting valid future data. Therefore, apply a one-sided custom BETWEEN-style constraint [0, ∞] (i.e., ENROLL12 >= 0) rather than strict observed bounds.

NUMTSTTAKR is a count of SAT test takers, so it is naturally non-negative and unbounded above in principle. A lower bound of 0 is semantically required, but the observed maximum of 24,305 comes from a finite snapshot and could be exceeded by larger schools or future data. Using a strict upper bound would risk rejecting valid future records, so a custom one-sided constraint [0, +∞] is more appropriate than the exact observed range.

This column is the average SAT Critical Reading score, which is naturally bounded by the SAT section score scale. Historically, SAT section scores range from 200 to 800 in 10-point increments, so any valid average must fall within [200, 800]. The observed range [308, 653] is narrower and reflects this particular dataset, not the true domain. Using strict bounds would incorrectly flag valid but unseen values (e.g., 250 or 700) as invalid. Therefore, a BETWEEN constraint with custom semantic bounds [200, 800] is appropriate.

AVGSCRMATH is an average SAT Math section score, which is naturally bounded by the SAT scale. For the classic SAT, section scores range from 200 to 800, so a semantic BETWEEN [200, 800] is appropriate. The observed range [289, 699] is narrower only because of this dataset’s particular schools and should not be enforced as a hard limit. Using custom bounds based on the known SAT scoring rules is safer and more accurate than strict bounds derived from current data.

AVGSCRWRITE is an average SAT writing score, which is naturally bounded by the SAT section score scale. The semantic range for SAT section scores is 200–800, so a BETWEEN constraint is appropriate. The observed range (312–671) likely reflects this particular dataset and not the true possible range of valid values. Using custom bounds [200, 800] is safer and more accurate than strict bounds, as it allows for valid but currently unobserved extreme scores while still catching impossible values.

NUMGE1500 is a count of students with SAT ≥1500, so it is naturally non-negative but has no fixed upper limit beyond total enrollment. The observed max of 5837 reflects current data, not a true semantic cap, and future schools or aggregations could exceed it. A safe constraint is a one-sided custom bound enforcing NUMGE1500 ≥ 0, without an upper BETWEEN limit.

DISTRICT_CODE is a coded identifier, not a numeric measure; it is naturally bounded to the set of valid district codes. The observed strict range [10017, 76901] is plausible for California district codes, while the IQR-based custom lower bound (50057) would incorrectly exclude many valid smaller codes. Since IDs are discrete and not subject to statistical outliers, an IQR-based bound is inappropriate. A two-sided BETWEEN using the strict observed bounds is the safer choice if a numeric range constraint is desired.

IRC is an integer flag column with only 0 and 1 observed, and no domain indication that other values are valid. It is semantically a binary indicator, so constraining it to [0, 1] is appropriate. Using custom bounds [0, 1] matches the strict observed range and clearly encodes the intended binary domain.

This is a coded status field for a specific year’s certification; in the data it only takes the value 1, and semantically it is a small, discrete code set rather than an open numeric measure. A BETWEEN constraint of [1, 1] (strict bounds) is appropriate to enforce the only valid code observed, while the custom bounds are identical here and offer no additional benefit.

STATUSTYPE is explicitly documented as a status enumeration with four defined values: Active, Closed, Merged, Pending. It represents a controlled vocabulary for district/school operational status, not free-form or expanding categories. Given the description lists these as the valid status types and they all appear in the data, an IN constraint on exactly these four values is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting unless the source specification itself changes in the future.

The description explicitly defines CHARTER as a binary indicator coded as 1 = charter school and 0 = not a charter school. This is a true, fully enumerated status flag with only two valid values by design, not a sparse numeric field. No additional codes are implied, so an IN constraint restricting values to {0, 1} is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting for future data.

FUNDINGTYPE is explicitly documented as an enumerated charter funding type with three text values: 'Not in CS (California School) funding model', 'Locally funded', and 'Directly funded'. The data shows exactly these three categories across 17,686 rows, which strongly suggests the sample is complete and reflects a controlled vocabulary, not free-form or expanding categories. While wording could theoretically change in future source systems, within this dataset and schema it is a true categorical/type field, so an IN constraint on these three values is appropriate and not overly limiting.

DOC is explicitly defined as a District Ownership Code with a fixed, documented set of numeric categories (00, 02, 03, 31, 34, 52, 54, 56, 98, etc.). This is a true code list, not free-form or open-ended data. The description lists specific allowed codes and their meanings, indicating a controlled vocabulary that should not arbitrarily expand. The presence of a small, stable set of values (12) over many rows further supports that this is an enumerated type. An IN constraint (possibly allowing for all documented codes, including any that appear in official specs but not in this sample) is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting if aligned with the official code list rather than just the observed values.

DOCTYPE is explicitly defined as the text description of the District Ownership Code (DOC), whose valid numeric codes and corresponding categories are enumerated in the documentation (e.g., County Office of Education, State Board of Education, Statewide Benefit Charter, Regional Occupational Center/Program, etc.). The observed 12 distinct text values align with those documented categories and represent a controlled vocabulary, not free-form text. While education agencies could theoretically introduce new ownership types in the future, in practice this set is stable and governed by policy. Given the small, well-defined, and semantically closed set of values, treating DOCTYPE as a categorical field with an IN constraint on the known values is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting for this dataset.

SOC is explicitly documented as a School Ownership Code with a fixed list of numeric codes (08, 09, 11, 13, 14, 15, 31, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 98). SOCTYPE is explicitly defined as the text description of the School Ownership Code (SOC), whose valid numeric codes and corresponding school types are enumerated in the documentation. The observed 20 distinct values align with those described categories (e.g., K-12 Schools (Public), High Schools (Public), ROC/ROP, etc.), indicating this is a controlled vocabulary, not an open‑ended text field. While minor spelling/label changes could occur, logically the domain is fixed to the set of school-type descriptions tied to SOC. An IN constraint (possibly allowing for known label variants/typos) is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting.

EDOPSCODE is explicitly documented as a short code for Educational Option Type with a fixed list of valid values (ALTSOC, COMM, COMMDAY, CON, JUV, OPP, YTH, SSS, SPEC, TRAD, ROP, HOMHOS, SPECON). EDOPSNAME is explicitly defined as an educational option name corresponding to a fixed set of education option codes (ALTSOC, COMM, COMMDAY, CON, JUV, OPP, YTH, SSS, SPEC, TRAD, ROP, HOMHOS, SPECON). The description lists these as a closed set of option types, and your observed 13 distinct values match that list (including the consortia special education variant). This is a true categorical/enumerated field, not free text or an open‑ended label, and new categories are unlikely without a formal change to the underlying code list. An IN constraint (or a reference to a lookup table with these 13 values) is appropriate and should not be too limiting; it will help catch data entry or mapping errors.

EILCODE is explicitly documented as an enumerated code with a fixed list of valid values: A, ELEM, ELEMHIGH, HS, INTMIDJR, PS, UG. The observed 7 unique values match this list exactly, and the field represents a controlled vocabulary (instruction level type), not free-form or expanding categories. EILNAME is explicitly defined as the long-text description of the Educational Instruction Level Code, whose valid codes are enumerated (A, ELEM, ELEMHIGH, HS, INTMIDJR, PS, UG). The seven observed values match exactly those descriptions: ['Adult', 'Elementary', 'Elementary-High Combination', 'High School', 'Intermediate/Middle/Junior High', 'Preschool', 'Ungraded']. This is a controlled vocabulary, not an open-ended text field, and new categories are unlikely without a formal change to the coding scheme. An IN constraint on these seven values (or the documented set) is appropriate and not overly limiting.

The documentation explicitly defines VIRTUAL as a coded categorical field with a fixed, known set of values: F (Exclusively Virtual), V (Primarily Virtual), C (Primarily Classroom), N (Not Virtual), and P (Partial Virtual, retired after 2016–17). This is a true enumeration, not free-form or open-ended. Even though the current data only shows ['P','N','F'], the spec clearly allows additional codes (V and C), so the IN constraint should be defined as the full documented set, not just the observed values. New categories are not expected beyond these documented codes, so an IN constraint on {F, V, C, N, P} is appropriate and not too limiting.

MAGNET is documented as a binary indicator: 1 = Magnet, 0 = Not Magnet. The description explicitly defines the only valid codes and does not suggest additional categories. The data shows exactly these two values across a large sample, reinforcing that it is a true boolean-style flag. New numeric categories are not expected, so an IN constraint on {0,1} is appropriate and not overly limiting.

RTYPE is clearly a small, fixed type code field (likely D = district, S = school) rather than free-form data. With only 2 values across the full SATSCORES table and a name that implies a record type flag, it is almost certainly an enumerated domain. Additional types (e.g., county, state) would typically be represented by other specific one-letter codes and would be known in advance; if they existed in this dataset, they would already appear. An IN constraint like CHECK (RTYPE IN ('D','S')) is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting unless the upstream data specification explicitly defines more RTYPE codes that are not present in this extract.

DISTRICT_TYPE is explicitly a type/category field for districts, and the observed values match the standard, finite set of California district organizational types (County Office of Education, State Board of Education, State Special Schools, Non-School Locations, Statewide Benefit Charter, and the three main district types). This is a controlled vocabulary, not free text or sparse data, and new types are unlikely to appear frequently. An IN constraint using this set (with allowance for future additions via schema change if needed) is appropriate and not overly limiting.

SCHOOL_TYPE is clearly a school classification/category field, not free-form text. The values align with the controlled list used in the SCHOOLS.SOC/SOCTYPE descriptions (e.g., Elementary Schools (Public), High Schools (Public), Continuation High Schools, Juvenile Court Schools, etc.). With 9,986 rows and only 17 distinct values, and given that these match a known statewide taxonomy of school types, this is a true enumerated domain rather than sparse data. While minor spelling/label variations could appear in other datasets, in this schema SCHOOL_TYPE is intended to be from a fixed set, so an IN constraint based on the official list of school types is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting.

The description for EDOPSCODE/EDOPSNAME in the SCHOOLS table lists a fixed set of educational option types (e.g., Alternative School of Choice, County Community School, Community Day School, Continuation School, Juvenile Court School, Youth Authority School, State Special School, Special Education School, Traditional, Regional Occupational Program, Home and Hospital, District Consortia Special Education School). The FRPM.EDUCATIONAL_OPTION_TYPE values you see are the long-text equivalents of that same controlled list. This is a true, administratively defined category field, not free-form text, and new categories are unlikely to appear frequently without a formal change in the code set. An IN constraint based on the official list of option types (not just the 12 observed values, but the full documented enumeration) is appropriate and should not be too limiting as long as it matches the authoritative code list.

NSLP_PROVISION_STATUS clearly represents a program/type code (Provision 1, Provision 2, Provision 3, CEP, etc.), which is a policy-defined status rather than free-form text. With 9,986 rows and only 7 distinct values, and all of them matching known NSLP provision models (including a catch-all 'Multiple Provision Types'), this is behaving as a controlled vocabulary. While future federal/state program changes could theoretically add new statuses, in practice these codes are stable and enumerated. An IN constraint on these known values is appropriate and would help catch data-entry errors; if new official provision types are ever introduced, the constraint can be updated at that time.

The description explicitly defines CHARTER_FUNDING_TYPE as an enumerated charter funding type with three text values: 'Not in CS (California School) funding model', 'Locally funded', and 'Directly funded'. The data shows exactly these three (with slightly shortened wording for the first), across nearly 10k rows, which strongly indicates a closed, code-list style domain rather than sparse free text. This is a stable classification field (a type/status), not something expected to grow arbitrarily, so an IN constraint on these three normalized values is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting, assuming you standardize the exact strings to match the official definitions.

Although the description says 'Not useful', the data pattern (exactly two integer values 0 and 1 across nearly 10k rows) strongly indicates a binary flag field rather than sparse numeric data. Binary indicator columns in these datasets are typically coded as 0/1 with no other valid codes. Given the size of the sample and the nature of similar fields (e.g., CHARTER, MAGNET), it is very likely that 0 and 1 are the complete, intended domain. An IN constraint on {0,1} is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting.

LOW_GRADE is an academic grade-level field, which is inherently drawn from a small, fixed set of valid grade codes (e.g., P/Preschool, K, 1–12, Adult). The data shows exactly those kinds of values and only 15 distinct codes across nearly 10k rows, which strongly suggests we are seeing the full controlled vocabulary rather than a sparse sample. Conceptually, new arbitrary values should not appear here (you don’t invent new grade labels ad hoc), so treating it as an enumerated categorical column and enforcing an IN constraint on the known grade codes is appropriate and not overly limiting.

HIGH_GRADE represents the highest grade level served (e.g., 'P', 'K', '1'–'13', 'Adult', 'Post Secondary'), which is inherently a small, fixed set of educational grade categories rather than arbitrary text. The description and the observed values align with standard K–12 plus preschool/adult/post-secondary designations, and it is unlikely that new, fundamentally different grade labels will appear. With 9,986 rows and only 17 distinct values, this is clearly an enumerated field, not sparse free-form data. An IN constraint over this controlled vocabulary is appropriate and unlikely to be too limiting, though it should explicitly include all known grade codes (P, K, 1–13, Adult, Post Secondary) rather than only those currently present in this sample if you want to future-proof it.

CDSCODE is the official statewide identifier (CDSCode) for each school and is effectively the primary key for the SCHOOLS table. Every school record must have a CDS code to be meaningful or joinable to other datasets (e.g., FRPM, SATSCORES). The description and usage indicate it is a fundamental identifier, not an optional attribute, and future valid records would not reasonably omit it. Therefore it should be enforced as NOT NULL (and ideally also as UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY).

STATUSTYPE is the core status indicator for each school/district (Active, Closed, Merged, Pending). The description frames it as an inherent property of every entity, not an optional attribute, and there is no alternative status field. All existing rows are populated, and any new school or district logically must have some status at creation. Allowing NULL would create ambiguous records (schools with no known status) and undermine filtering/logic that depends on status. Therefore it should be enforced as NOT NULL.

COUNTY is a core geographic identifier for each school and is part of the standard CDS context (county–district–school). The description does not indicate it is optional, and every existing record has a value. For any valid school record, it is not meaningful to omit the county, and future schools will necessarily belong to some county. This is not a secondary or convenience field like an abbreviation or mailing variant; it is a primary attribute of the school’s identity and location, so enforcing NOT NULL is appropriate.

DISTRICT is the district name for each school and is a core identifier in this dataset. Every school logically belongs to some district-level administrative authority (including county offices or special programs), and the official documentation treats it as a standard attribute, not an optional one. There is no indication that some schools would legitimately lack a district/authority name, and all existing records are populated. Future records without a district name would be incomplete and of limited use, so enforcing NOT NULL is appropriate.

DOC is a core categorical identifier (District Ownership Code) that classifies the administrative authority type for every district/school. The description presents it as a required code with a defined, closed set of values and no indication that it is optional; it is fundamental to interpreting the record, not a secondary attribute. All existing rows are non-null, and future schools/districts will also need an ownership category to be valid in this schema. It is unlikely that a legitimate record would lack any DOC value, so enforcing NOT NULL is appropriate.

DOCTYPE is the textual description of DOC (the district ownership code), which categorizes the administrative authority for every school/district. Conceptually, every record must belong to exactly one ownership category for the dataset to be meaningful, and the sample values show it is consistently populated for all existing rows. The description does not indicate that this field is optional or only applicable to certain entities, unlike other fields where missing data is explicitly allowed. While DOC could theoretically stand alone as the required code, in this schema DOCTYPE is treated as a core classification attribute that is always present, so enforcing NOT NULL is appropriate and unlikely to conflict with valid future records.

LASTUPDATE is a system/metadata field indicating when the record was last updated; such audit fields are typically expected for every row. The description does not suggest it is optional, and the fact that 100% of existing rows have a value supports that it is treated as required in practice. Future records should always have an update timestamp for data integrity and auditing, so allowing NULL would be more likely to indicate bad or incomplete data than a legitimate absence of a value.

CDS is the California Department of Education’s school/district identifier and functions as the core key tying SAT score records to specific schools or districts. Without a CDS value, a SATSCORES row could not be meaningfully linked to any entity, making the record unusable. The description and naming indicate it is an essential identifier, not an optional attribute, and all existing rows are non-null in a way that reflects this logical requirement rather than coincidence. Future SAT score records without a CDS code would not be valid, so a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

RTYPE appears to be a required record-type flag (e.g., S=school, D=district) that defines what the row represents. Every existing row has it populated, and without it the meaning and level of aggregation of the record would be ambiguous. It is not a secondary or optional attribute but a core classifier for each row, so future records should also always specify it. A NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

DNAME is the district name, a descriptive attribute tied to the school/district, not a key or core identifier. The true identifier is CDS (and possibly RTYPE). While current data happens to be complete, there is no strong logical requirement that every SAT score record must have a district name; future records could reasonably omit it (e.g., incomplete source data, aggregate or special records). Therefore it should remain nullable despite 100% non-null in the current dataset.

CNAME is a descriptive county name field, not a key or essential identifier. The true identifier is likely CDS (and possibly RTYPE), and analyses can still be done using those even if CNAME is missing. The description does not state it is mandatory, and it is easy to imagine future rows where the county name is unknown, derived later, or intentionally omitted (e.g., aggregate or test rows). The fact that current data is 100% populated suggests good data quality, not a logical requirement, so enforcing NOT NULL would be unnecessarily strict.

ENROLL12 is a descriptive metric (12th-grade enrollment), not a key or core identifier. The description does not state it is mandatory, and it is easy to imagine future rows where enrollment is unknown, not yet reported, or not applicable (e.g., aggregate or placeholder records). The fact that current data happens to be 100% populated does not imply a logical requirement, so enforcing NOT NULL could block valid future records with missing enrollment data.

This column is the number of SAT test takers for the record and is essential to interpreting all the other SAT-related metrics (e.g., NUMGE1500 and any derived rates). A record without NUMTSTTAKR would be analytically meaningless, and the data definition treats it as a core measure, not an optional attribute. The presence of 0 as a valid value already covers the case of no test takers, so NULL is not needed to represent that situation. Given its role as a fundamental count field and the fact that every existing row has a value, it should be required and constrained as NOT NULL.

CDSCODE is the core statewide school identifier (CDSCode) and functions as the natural key tying FRPM records to the SCHOOLS table and other datasets. Every FRPM row represents data for a specific school/year and must be associated with a valid school; a record without a CDSCODE would be unusable and not meaningfully linkable. The description does not indicate it is optional, and identifiers of this type are logically required for every record, so future records should not omit it. The fact that 100% of existing rows are non-null is consistent with this logical requirement rather than a coincidence.

ACADEMIC_YEAR is a core identifier for each FRPM record: it indicates which school year the enrollment and meal-eligibility metrics apply to. Without it, the record’s data (counts, percentages) would be ambiguous and unusable for time-based analysis. The description treats it as a defining attribute, not an optional note, and all existing rows are non-null, consistent with it being logically required. It is very unlikely that a valid FRPM record could exist without a known academic year, so a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

COUNTY_CODE is a core geographic identifier for each FRPM record and is part of the standard CDS breakdown (county–district–school). The description treats it as a fundamental code, not an optional attribute, and FRPM records are inherently tied to a specific county. While 100% non-null alone doesn’t prove necessity, the semantics of the field and its role in uniquely and consistently identifying the school’s jurisdiction make it logically required; future valid FRPM records should not exist without a county code. Therefore a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

DISTRICT_CODE is a core identifier for each FRPM record, used to locate the record within the state’s county–district–school coding structure. As a key part of the district identity (and likely used in joins to other tables or to external reference data), it is logically required for every row. The description does not suggest it is optional, and FRPM data is typically reported at the district/school level, which inherently requires a district code. While some records might represent county- or state-level aggregates, those would normally use a special code rather than a null. Given its role as an essential identifier and the fact that all existing rows are non-null, it should be constrained NOT NULL.

SCHOOL_CODE is a core identifier in the FRPM dataset (paired with COUNTY_CODE and DISTRICT_CODE and embedded in CDSCODE). Conceptually every school-level FRPM record must correspond to a specific school, so a missing school code would make the record unusable and non-joinable to other school datasets. The description and naming indicate it is a standard CDE school identifier, not an optional attribute, and there is no scenario where an FRPM record without a school code would be meaningful. The fact that 100% of existing rows are non-null aligns with this logical requirement rather than looking coincidental, so a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

COUNTY_NAME is a core identifier for each FRPM record and is conceptually required: every school/district in this dataset must belong to a county. The description does not indicate it is optional, and the sample values show it is a standard, well-defined attribute (not something like a secondary contact). It is also part of the basic location/identity set alongside COUNTY_CODE, DISTRICT_NAME, and SCHOOL_NAME. While the code field (COUNTY_CODE) could theoretically stand alone, in practice this dataset is clearly designed to always carry the human-readable county name, and there is no plausible case where a valid record would have a county code but no county name. Given 100% completeness and the logical requirement that every record belongs to a county, a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

DISTRICT_NAME is a core identifier for each FRPM record: every row is tied to a specific district, and the name is part of the human-readable identity alongside codes like COUNTY_CODE and DISTRICT_CODE. The description does not indicate it is optional, and it would be unusual and confusing to have an FRPM record with no district name even if the numeric codes are present. Given that all existing 9,986 rows are non-null and the field is semantically essential for interpretation and reporting, it is reasonable to enforce a NOT NULL constraint; future records without a district name would likely be considered incomplete or invalid data rather than acceptable omissions.

SCHOOL_NAME is a core identifier for each FRPM record and is expected to exist whenever a school-level record exists. The description treats it as a fundamental attribute (like COUNTY_NAME and DISTRICT_NAME), not an optional note, and there is no indication that some school records would legitimately lack a name. While CDSCODE is the true key, a school without a name would be practically unusable in reporting and analysis. Given that all existing rows are non-null and the semantics of the field, it is reasonable to enforce NOT NULL for SCHOOL_NAME.

DISTRICT_TYPE is a core categorical attribute describing what kind of district entity each FRPM record belongs to (e.g., Unified, High School, COE, State Board). Every record represents some educational entity that, by definition, must fall into one of these types for reporting and interpretation. The description does not indicate it is optional, and analyses of FRPM data (grouping, filtering, compliance reporting) generally assume a valid district type for every row. While the current 100% completeness alone is not proof, the semantics of the field make it logically required for any valid record, and there is no clear, realistic case where a legitimate FRPM row would have an unknown or inapplicable district type. Therefore a NOT NULL constraint is appropriate.

LOW_GRADE represents the lowest grade offered by the school/district, which is a core attribute of each FRPM record. The description treats it as part of the basic definition of the institution (grade span), not as an optional or occasionally missing field, and there is no indication that some schools would legitimately lack a lowest grade (even preschool/adult are encoded with values like P). All existing 9986 records have values, and future FRPM records describing a school without any defined lowest grade would be logically inconsistent. Therefore this column should be required and constrained as NOT NULL.

HIGH_GRADE is part of the core definition of a school’s grade span (paired with LOW_GRADE) and is not described as optional; every school logically has a highest grade it serves, and the dataset is designed around reporting K–12/Adult enrollment by school. The fact that 100% of existing rows are populated, combined with its role as an essential attribute rather than a secondary or contact field, suggests it is a required property for each FRPM record. Future records without a defined highest grade would be incomplete and likely invalid for this dataset’s purpose, so enforcing NOT NULL is appropriate.

This field is a one-off, year-specific status flag (for the 2013–14 CALPADS Fall 1 certification). It is not a key, not needed to identify a record, and not fundamental to the FRPM record’s existence. The description does not state it is mandatory, and future FRPM records for other academic years could reasonably omit or not apply this 2013–14-specific status. The fact that the current dataset happens to have 100% non-null values is likely incidental to this particular extract, not evidence of a logical requirement, so enforcing NOT NULL would be unnecessarily strict.

CDSCODE is effectively a unique school identifier, so it will trivially determine NCESDIST along with every other column in the row. While each school belongs to exactly one NCES district at a point in time, that relationship is already implied by CDSCODE being a key and could change historically (e.g., district reorganizations or NCES reassignments). This is not a semantic code→label mapping but a key→attribute mapping, so adding CDSCODE → NCESDIST as a separate functional dependency constraint provides little additional value and may be brittle over time.

CDSCODE is effectively a unique school identifier, so it will (trivially) determine every other column, including NCESSCHOOL. That makes the observed dependency CDSCODE → NCESSCHOOL more a consequence of CDSCODE being a key than a meaningful semantic mapping. Semantically, NCESDist + NCESSCHOOL together form the NCES school ID; CDSCODE is a different coding system, and there is no strong guarantee that the crosswalk between state and federal IDs will always be one-to-one or permanently stable (e.g., NCES IDs can change, be added later, or be null for some CDSCODEs). Enforcing this as a functional dependency adds little value beyond the primary-key uniqueness of CDSCODE and could be brittle if NCES identifiers are updated or backfilled, so it should not be enforced as a separate constraint.

CDSCODE is effectively a unique school identifier, so it will (trivially) determine STATUSTYPE along with every other attribute in the row. While the mapping is 100% consistent in the current 17,686 rows, this is not a semantic code→description relationship but simply a primary-key-like identifier determining one of many attributes. Enforcing CDSCODE → STATUSTYPE adds little value beyond the uniqueness of CDSCODE and could be brittle if historical records or status changes were ever modeled differently (e.g., multiple records per CDSCODE over time). It is therefore a trivial/structural dependency rather than a meaningful semantic constraint and should not be added as a separate functional dependency constraint.

CDSCODE is effectively a unique school identifier, and as such it trivially determines all school attributes, including COUNTY. While the mapping is 100% consistent and semantically real (the county is encoded in the CDS code), modeling CDSCODE → COUNTY as a separate functional dependency adds little value beyond the primary-key semantics and would create noise. It is better treated as part of the general rule that CDSCODE uniquely identifies the row, rather than as a standalone constraint.
